questions.prompt: The rank of a matrix is…
questions.explanation: Rank is the dimension of the column space, which equals the dimension of the row space. Duplicate rows do not add to it, so rank need not equal the row count. The product of the diagonal entries is not the determinant once there are off-diagonal terms, and it is not the rank. The largest entry is a size, not a count of independent directions.

questions.explanation:
For \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\) the determinant is \(ad-bc = 2\cdot 3 - 1\cdot 0 = 6\). It is also the product of the eigenvalues. This matrix is triangular, so those eigenvalues are the diagonal entries \(2\) and \(3\).
• \(2+3 = 5\) is the trace, the sum of the eigenvalues, not the product.
• \(2 	imes 1 	imes 3 = 6\) happens to match only because the off-diagonal \(0\) drops out. Including a nonzero \(c\) that way would be wrong.
• \(1\) is an entry, not the determinant.

questions.prompt: The null space of a matrix \(A\) is the set of vectors \(x\) such that…
questions.explanation: The null space is every \(x\) that \(A\) sends to the zero vector. The set of all \(Av\) is the column space, a different object. Eigenvalues are scalars, not the vectors in the null space, though a zero eigenvalue means the null space is nontrivial. A row of \(A\) is not, in general, sent to zero.

questions.prompt: What is the larger eigenvalue of \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation:
The trace is \(7\) and the determinant is \(12-2 = 10\). The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda-5)(\lambda-2)\). The eigenvalues are \(5\) and \(2\). The larger one is \(5\).
• \(7\) is the trace, the sum, not the larger root.
• \(10\) is the determinant, the product.
• \(2\) is the other eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: If \(B = P^{-1} A P\) with \(P\) invertible, what must \(A\) and \(B\) share?
questions.explanation: This is a similarity transform, a change of coordinates. If \(Av = \lambda v\), then \(B(P^{-1}v) = \lambda (P^{-1}v)\). The eigenvalues match. The eigenvectors are the same geometric directions only after they are rewritten in the new coordinates. The matrices are equal only when \(P\) commutes in a trivial way. The determinant is preserved because it is the product of the eigenvalues, so preserving the determinant is weaker than, and a consequence of, preserving the eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: How many dimensions does the null space of \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) have?
questions.explanation:
The second row is twice the first, so the rank is \(1\). A \(2\)-column matrix then has nullity \(2 - 1 = 1\). One null vector is \((2,-1)\), since \(1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot(-1) = 0\). It is not the zero matrix, so the nullity is not \(2\).
• \(0\) would mean the two columns are independent, but the second column is twice the first.
• \(2\) would mean every vector is sent to zero.
• \(4\) is an entry, not a dimension.

questions.explanation:
The equations are \(3x + y = 5\) and \(x + 2y = 4\). From the second, \(x = 4 - 2y\). Substitute: \(3(4-2y) + y = 5\), so \(12 - 5y = 5\), \(y = 1.4\), and \(x = 4 - 2.8 = 1.2\). Check: \(3(1.2)+1.4 = 5\) and \(1.2+2(1.4) = 4\).
• \(1.4\) is \(y\), not \(x\).
• \(5/3 = 1.667\) drops the second unknown.
• \(4/2 = 2\) does the same with the other equation.

questions.prompt: A \(2 \times 2\) matrix has trace \(5\) and determinant \(6\). Which polynomial is \(\det(A - \lambda I)\), up to the conventional sign that makes the leading term \(+\lambda^2\)? More usefully: the characteristic polynomial \(\det(\lambda I - A)\) is…
questions.explanation: \(\det(\lambda I - A) = \lambda^2 - (\mathrm{tr}\, A)\lambda + \det(A)\). With trace \(5\) and determinant \(6\) that is \(\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6\). A plus sign on the trace term flips every eigenvalue's sign. Swapping trace and determinant mixes the sum of the roots with their product. A minus on the determinant makes the product of the roots negative, which a positive determinant forbids.

questions.prompt: The eigenvalues of \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\) are real and negative. Which one is closer to zero?
questions.explanation:
The trace is \(-3\) and the determinant is \(2\). Then \(\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = (\lambda+1)(\lambda+2)\). The roots are \(-1\) and \(-2\). The one closer to zero is \(-1\).
• \(-2\) is the faster mode.
• \(-3\) is the trace, the sum of the roots.
• \(+1\) flips the sign. Both roots are in the left half-plane.

questions.prompt: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the controllability matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} B & AB \end{bmatrix}\). What is its rank?
questions.explanation: \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}\), so the controllability matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(-1\), not zero, so the rank is \(2\). Full rank is the reachability test for a two-state linear system.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>A 2 by 2 controllability matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0               1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1           -   2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 0, 1 and second row 1, -2.

questions.prompt: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), the observability matrix stacks \(C\) over \(CA\). What is its rank?
questions.explanation: \(CA = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Stacking gives \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The second row is \(-1\) times the first, and the second column is zero, so the rank is \(1\), not \(2\). A rank short of the state dimension means the pair is not observable: the mode at \(-3\) never appears in the output.

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 1, 0 and second row -1, 0.

questions.prompt: Pole placement wants the closed-loop characteristic polynomial \((s+2)(s+5)\). What is the coefficient of \(s\)?
questions.explanation:
\((s+2)(s+5) = s^2 + 7s + 10\). The coefficient of \(s\) is the sum of the desired poles, \(2+5 = 7\). State feedback chooses a gain so the closed-loop matrix has exactly this characteristic polynomial.
• \(10\) is the constant term, the product of the poles.
• \(2\) or \(5\) is one pole, not the sum.
• \(-7\) flips the sign that the monic polynomial \(\det(sI - A)\) uses.
